opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at in some follow-up work, where we tried to see whether the time-horizon trend we found on our own task suite generalizes to other domains. Computer use, things like OSWorld, was one of the more interesting cases, because it looks pretty different from our tasks.

The headline is that the time horizons for computer-use tasks are quite a bit shorter. Models that can handle tasks taking a human expert maybe an hour or more on our mostly text-based software and research tasks tend to succeed only on much shorter tasks when they have to operate a GUI: clicking around, reading screenshots, navigating applications. The absolute level is lower by a pretty substantial factor.

What I find more interesting is that the rate of improvement looked roughly similar. The doubling time seemed to be in the same ballpark as what we see elsewhere, with the line shifted down. I'd hold that loosely, since there's less data and the benchmarks weren't designed with time-horizon measurement in mind. We had to estimate human completion times somewhat indirectly, and that adds a lot of noise.

As for why the level is lower, my guess is that a lot of it comes down to perception and interface skills: grounding, knowing exactly where to click, dealing with UIs that weren't built for models. Those are bottlenecks somewhat separate from the reasoning and planning abilities our tasks stress. Humans find that stuff trivial, so tasks that take a person thirty seconds can still trip models up, which compresses the measured horizon.

So my takeaway is that the time-horizon framing seems to carry over reasonably well. You still get a fairly clean relationship between how long a task takes humans and whether models succeed. But you can't take a single number like "models can do two-hour tasks" and apply it across domains. It's domain-specific, and computer use is currently one of the weaker areas. If the trends hold, you'd expect it to keep improving at a similar pace, just from a lower starting point. And it could catch up faster if the perception bottlenecks get solved, since that would be more of a one-time jump than a gradual trend.

r001.rationale: The response says the computer-use horizon doubling time was “in the same ballpark” as what they see elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It states computer-use time horizons are “quite a bit shorter” and that the absolute level is lower by a “substantial factor” than on mostly text-based tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a fair amount, and I want to be careful here because I think the headline comparison can be a little misleading in both directions.

So the basic observation is that if you take the METR time-horizon methodology and apply it to something like OSWorld, you get horizons that are way shorter than what you see on METR's suite. On the software engineering and research-style tasks, the 50% horizon is now in the range of hours, and on computer-use tasks it's more like minutes. And the naive read is, okay, models are just much worse at computer use, there's some big gap.

I think that's partly true, but I'd flag a few things.

The first is that the human baselines are measuring really different things. When METR times a human on a coding task, that's an experienced engineer who's thinking, planning, reading documentation, debugging. A lot of the task time is cognitive. When you time a human on an OSWorld task, a huge fraction of the time is just, like, moving the mouse, waiting for a window to load, clicking through menus. So a "ten minute" OSWorld task might have way less actual reasoning in it than a ten minute coding task. The time axis isn't really a shared unit of difficulty across the two benchmarks. So I'd be hesitant to put them on the same plot and say "look, computer use is three years behind."

The second thing is that the failure modes look different. On the agentic coding tasks, when models fail on long tasks, it's often because they lose track of state, or they make a bad high-level decision early and never recover. On computer-use tasks, a lot of the failures are much more mundane. The model misreads a pixel-level UI element, it clicks slightly wrong, it doesn't notice a dialog popped up. Those are more like perception and grounding problems than reasoning or planning problems. And my guess is those get fixed in a kind of different way, and possibly faster, because they're more amenable to just scaling up the right kind of training data, rather than requiring some deeper capability.

Third, I think OSWorld specifically has a lot of noise in the task set. Some of the tasks are just kind of broken or underspecified, there are tasks where the evaluation checks something really brittle. METR put a lot of effort into making sure their tasks were actually doable and that the baselines were meaningful, and I don't think OSWorld had the same level of scrutiny initially, though it's been improved. So some of the gap is benchmark quality, not model capability.

That said, I don't want to fully explain it away. I do think there's a real gap. Models have had enormous amounts of optimization pressure on coding, both in pretraining and in RL, and much less on actually operating a GUI. And there's a real question about whether the doubling-time story holds across domains. If you only measure the thing the labs are most focused on, you might get a rosier picture of general agentic capability than is warranted.

So the thing I'd actually want is more text-only-style versus computer-use-style comparisons where the tasks are matched on the underlying cognitive demand, and then see if the horizons diverge. My prior is that the gap is real but smaller than the raw numbers suggest, and that it closes relatively quickly once people care about it. But I hold that loosely.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the doubling-time story holds across domains, but does not state that the doubling times appeared similar.

r002.rationale: It says OSWorld horizons are “way shorter” than METR’s, describing hours for software engineering and research tasks versus minutes for computer-use tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re a useful caution about how to interpret the METR results. A human taking an hour on a task doesn’t necessarily mean that task presents the same difficulty for an AI as another task that takes a human an hour. The interface matters a lot. With computer use, you have to interpret what’s on the screen, take an action, and then figure out whether that action did what you intended. That can introduce failure modes that aren’t as prominent when you’re working with text or code.

So I wouldn’t take a time horizon measured on METR’s tasks and straightforwardly apply it to OSWorld, or to office work in general. But I also wouldn’t take worse performance on computer-use tasks as showing that the underlying capabilities aren’t improving. It could partly reflect a bottleneck in interacting with the environment.

What I’d really want to see is the trend within each setting. Are computer-use time horizons increasing at a similar rate, just from a lower starting point? Or is reliable interaction imposing a different constraint? Those would lead me to fairly different conclusions. The time-horizon framing is useful, but I think we should treat it as a property of a model on a particular distribution of tasks, rather than a single number that tells us how long it can work autonomously on anything.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether computer-use time horizons are increasing at a similar rate, but does not state that their doubling time appeared similar to METR’s.

r002.rationale: It mentions worse computer-use performance and a possible lower starting point, but does not state that measured absolute time horizons were substantially shorter than METR’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is that the time horizon is a property of the model and the task distribution together. It’s not just a number you can assign to a model independently of how you’re evaluating it.

With computer-use tasks, you can have something that takes a human only a few minutes but requires a lot of individual actions from the model. And each of those is an opportunity to make a mistake: click in the wrong place, misunderstand what’s on the screen, or fail to notice that an action didn’t work. So a shorter horizon on OSWorld could reflect those interface difficulties rather than an inability to carry out a plan of that duration.

Conversely, in a text-based environment, the model can often do quite a lot with a single command. That makes human completion time a somewhat different measure of difficulty across the two settings.

So I’d be cautious about taking the METR results and interpreting them as saying that a model can reliably do any computer task that takes a human that long. The results are useful, but I’d want to look at the trends within each benchmark and understand the failure modes before treating the horizons as directly comparable.
